title: Multi-cursor editing
summary: Edit many places at once with Ctrl+D, Alt+Click, column selection and cursors above and below, then make the keys your own.

steps.title: Many cursors, one edit
body: Multi-cursor is VS Code's answer to Vim's `.` and `:s`: put a cursor in every place that needs the same change, then type once.
| Add the next match of the selection | `Ctrl+D` | `Ctrl+D` | `Cmd+D` |
| Add a cursor where you click | `Alt+Click` | `Alt+Click` | `Option+Click` |
| Skip this match, go to the next | `Ctrl+K Ctrl+D` | `Ctrl+K Ctrl+D` | `Cmd+K Cmd+D` |
`Ctrl+D` is the one to learn first: select a word (or press `Ctrl+D` once with the cursor in it), then each `Ctrl+D` adds the next occurrence. You see every match before you change it.

steps.prompt: Match the macOS shortcut to what it does.
pairs: add the next match to the selection
add a cursor where you click
add a cursor on the line below
undo the last cursor you added

steps.prompt: Which keys add a cursor on the line below, on each system?

You want to rename the local variable `cnt` to `count` in one function, but `cnt` also appears in `cntMax` and in a comment you want to keep. You put the cursor on the first `cnt` and press `Ctrl+D` repeatedly. What do you press when the selection lands on the comment?
options: `Ctrl+K Ctrl+D`: skip it and move to the next match
steps.explain: `Ctrl+K Ctrl+D` moves the last selection to the next match instead of adding it. With the cursor in a word and nothing selected, `Ctrl+D` matches whole words only, so `cntMax` is never picked. For a real rename, `F2` is still the safer tool.

steps.prompt: Turn five lines of host names into quoted, comma-separated strings (`"web1",`) with multi-cursor on Windows. Put the steps in order.
lines: Click at the start of the first host name
Press `Ctrl+Alt+Down` four times (one cursor per line)
Press `End`: every cursor jumps to the end of its own line
Press `Esc` to go back to one cursor

steps.title: Make the keys your own
body: Shortcuts live in `keybindings.json`, next to your user `settings.json` (on Linux `~/.config/Code/User/`). `Ctrl+K Ctrl+S` (`Cmd+K Cmd+S`) opens the editor for them; the palette command **Preferences: Open Keyboard Shortcuts (JSON)** opens the file. Each entry names a key, a command ID and, optionally, a `when` clause:

One setting changes multi-cursor itself: `"editor.multiCursorModifier": "ctrlCmd"` makes `Ctrl+Click` (`Cmd+Click`) add cursors and moves *Go to definition* to `Alt+Click`. Teams coming from other editors often switch it.

steps.prompt: Complete the user settings so `Ctrl+Click` adds cursors and files are saved automatically when you switch away.

steps.title: Your own settings and a keybinding
prompt: VS Code on Linux keeps your user settings in `~/.config/Code/User/`. That folder already has a `settings.json` with your font size.
2. Create `keybindings.json` there with one binding: `ctrl+alt+d` runs `editor.action.copyLinesDownAction` when `editorTextFocus`.
`jq` is handy for editing JSON safely: `jq '. + {"key": "value"}' file > tmp && mv tmp file`. (Real VS Code files may contain comments, which `jq` cannot read; these do not.)

checks.name: settings.json has ctrlCmd and still has the font size
checks.fail: `settings.json` should have `editor.multiCursorModifier` set to `ctrlCmd` and still `editor.fontSize` 14.

checks.name: keybindings.json binds ctrl+alt+d
checks.fail: `keybindings.json` must be a JSON **array** of entries, with one `{ "key": "ctrl+alt+d", "command": "editor.action.copyLinesDownAction", "when": "editorTextFocus" }`.

hints: `cd ~/.config/Code/User` first. `jq '. + {"editor.multiCursorModifier": "ctrlCmd"}' settings.json > s.tmp && mv s.tmp settings.json`.
`keybindings.json` is an array: it starts with `[` and holds objects with `key`, `command` and `when`.
solution: jq '. + {"editor.multiCursorModifier": "ctrlCmd"}' settings.json > s.tmp && mv s.tmp settings.json
steps.explain: Keep these two files in your dotfiles repo, or turn on **Settings Sync** (it syncs settings, keybindings, extensions and snippets through your GitHub or Microsoft account). Command IDs, like `editor.action.copyLinesDownAction`, are shown in the Keyboard Shortcuts editor: right-click a command and choose **Copy Command ID**.
